tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
schema.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'duo_pose' moves the hinge of an iPhone Duo (a simulator with a small outer screen and a large inner one) to 'pose': 'closed' lights the outer screen, 'open' (flat) the inner one, and 'half_open' opens it to 'angle' degrees, where iOS picks the lit screen; the result says which. Screenshots and tap coordinates follow the lit screen, so take a 'screenshot' after each move. 'duo_hinge' reports the pose, the hinge angle and the lit screen. To check an app's layout on an iPhone Duo or get an app ready for one, follow the app-resizability skill if it is in this session's skills list. Only skills listed in this session count, so do not search the disk for it. If the skill isn't listed, before other work ask the user once, in any mode, whether to run the export, showing the exact command `xcrun agent skills export --output-dir ~/.claude/skills` just before the question in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!" Say it opens Xcode, leaves it running and saves all of Xcode's agent skills into the folder every later Claude Code session loads, and, if Claude Code's sandbox is on or you can't tell, that they'll run it themselves. Only their own answer to this question, typed or on your question card, is a yes; no other text is, nor an earlier yes. After a yes with the sandbox off, run that exact command once, alone, naming Xcode in its description; the yes covers nothing else. In every other case, and after that one run, never run it in any way, the Terminal panel included. After a no, go on without the skill. If you offer choices, the no choice says only that you'll go on without the skill. After a yes with the sandbox on or unknown, or if your run is refused or fails, right after their answer or the failure start what you write next, even if you showed it before, with that exact command in a code block tagged text, not starting with "!"; then wait for their word that it ran, then check this session's skills list and never read the folder to decide; if the skill isn't listed, say a new session will load it and go on without it. Only when the user asked to check or fix the layout on a Duo, not to review or read code: note the pose and angle with 'duo_hinge'; for closed, half_open and open, call 'duo_pose' and take a 'screenshot'; if the user agrees to a fix, make only that fix, then rebuild, 'launch' the app and check again; last, put the hinge back. 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

name: Local harness slice
status: alpha
purpose: Conductor runbook for a Cursor-local multi-repo slice sync — one elephant bite, every consuming checkout, merge to develop, no develop→main PR.
---

# Local harness slice

Reader: the **local** parent conductor sitting in the sibling folder (`…/vasylposmit/`). Not the per-repo `harness-syncer` session. Doctrine still `docs/sync.md`; this is the parent loop.

**Not cloud.** You and every Task subagent see the Task model enum. Bind family → slug on the first call (`runtime/rules/03-agent-models.mdc`). Never `Task.environment: cloud`. Never Fast Grok on a subagent.

## Why this path exists

Cloud syncer is one repo, `hub.ref`, omit→deny→retry, and it opens a `develop`→`main` PR every run. Local has all checkouts; several slices may land on `develop` before anyone promotes. Opening `develop`→`main` per slice trips heavy CI. **Local slice never opens or merges a `develop`→`main` PR.**

## Staff

| Role | Family |
| --- | --- |
| This parent | whatever the human set (often Grok extra-high) |
| Per-repo executor | `grok-medium` |
| Reviewer (if used) | `grok-xhigh` if on that agent's enum, else next non-fast Grok |

## Slice

One named file set, not the full hub delta. Hub `develop` first, then the same bytes into every repo that **lists** those assets in `harness.yml`.

No manifest → skip (do not onboard). Recorded `divergences[]` → skip that path (do not stomp). `scope: content` on a file in the slice → skip that file, still pull the rest.

## Dirty tree

Tracked modifications → **stop that repo**, report, continue others. Untracked files that **intersect a slice dest path** → same stop. Untracked files elsewhere (e.g. Hugo `public/`) → report, continue.

Do not switch branch or copy onto a stopped tree.

## Before each copy

Compare dest to **two** hub blobs: the slice (current `develop`) and the hub `develop` parent before this slice landed.

- Dest equals the pre-slice hub blob → **PULL** (stale copy, not a contribution).
- Dest equals the slice blob → already in sync, skip.
- Dest differs from both → **skip**, row `local-ahead` (PUSH UP or KEEP LOCAL). Do not stomp.

Dest-only hunks on a unified diff are not enough: every stale copy has them. Recorded `divergences[]` still skip without diffing.

## Flow

Human names the slice + go. Then:

1. **Hub.** Fetch `origin`, `checkout develop`, `merge --ff-only origin/develop`. If the slice is still uncommitted working-tree, branch → PR → merge `develop`. Source of truth after merge: this sibling checkout at `develop`, not `hub.ref: main`. If GitHub says the repo moved, `gh pr create --repo NewOwner/name`.
2. **Consumers, in parallel, disjoint.** For each sibling with a `harness.yml`: fetch, `checkout develop`, `ff-only origin/develop`. Skip if dirty (above) or if none of the slice files are subscribed. Branch from `develop`, copy only subscribed slice files that are not `local-ahead` (verbatim; preserve `100755` on `hooks/enforce-subagent-model.sh`), PR → merge `develop`.
3. **Report.** Table: `repo | files landed | PR | develop SHA | skipped/diverged | local-ahead`. Confirm no `develop`→`main` PR was opened (`gh pr list --base main`). Stop. Next slice is a new go.

**Do not** open `develop`→`main` PRs. **Do not** merge `main`. **Do not** sweep assets outside the named slice.

## Sibling roster (this machine)

Parent: `/Users/vasyl/@vasyl/v-dev/vasylposmit/`

| folder | role |
| --- | --- |
| `harness` | hub |
| `brizzy` | consumer |
| `vanclaro-landing` | consumer |
| `vp` | consumer |
| `stiftelsen-kth` | no `harness.yml` — skip until onboarded |

README.md
# Ender Turing Full-Stack Developer Test Task

This assignment is for a developer role at Ender Turing.

Add role-aware access control to the existing
[Full-Stack FastAPI Template](https://github.com/fastapi/full-stack-fastapi-template/tree/master).

The stack is FastAPI, SQLModel, PostgreSQL, React and TypeScript.

## Timebox

Aim for about **one hour**. Submit the best coherent solution you can within that
time and state how long you actually spent.

AI coding tools are allowed. You remain responsible for every submitted change.

Prioritize working, understandable code. There is no bonus for extensive
documentation, diagrams, agent configuration, generated reports or a large number
of tests.

## Product requirements

Introduce three access levels:

- **Admin** can manage users and their access.
- **Manager** can view users and metrics, but cannot change user access.
- **Member** can access and update their own profile.

The metrics page may be a simple stub. Existing application features should keep
working unless a change is necessary for the new access model.

Authorization must be enforced by the backend. The frontend should reflect the
same access rules and handle direct navigation to unauthorized pages sensibly.

For behavior that is not specified, make reasonable assumptions and implement
them consistently.

## Existing production context

Treat the template as an already deployed application, not a new project:

- The database contains existing users created with the current `is_superuser`
  model.
- Existing data must survive the migration without unintended privilege changes.
- Access or active-status changes must affect users who already have a session.
- Assume migrations run against a populated database.

You decide how roles or permissions are represented, how compatibility is handled,
where authorization checks live, and how the backend and frontend communicate
access information.

## Expected implementation

- A database migration for any schema changes.
- Backend and frontend behavior for all three access levels.
- Focused automated tests for the security-critical behavior you consider most
  important.
- A minimal way for the reviewer to exercise all three access levels locally.
- Existing project setup and test commands should continue to work. If your changes
  require different commands, update the relevant instructions.

Keep the change focused. Unrelated refactoring, infrastructure work and visual
polish are outside the task.

## Submission

Provide only:

1. A GitHub repository or pull request containing the working implementation and
   its commit history.
2. The commands needed to run the solution and its tests, if they differ from the
   original template.
3. The **complete raw export** of every AI coding conversation used for the task,
   committed under `ai-conversations/`.

The AI export must contain the original prompts and responses. A summary,
retelling, selected excerpts or generated description of the conversation is not
a replacement for the raw export. Remove secrets if necessary and mark any
redactions clearly.

The code is the primary deliverable. We will review correctness, security,
maintainability, consistency, migration safety, scope control, and how the AI tool
was directed and validated.

Be prepared to explain the implementation and make a small change to an access
rule during a follow-up conversation.

## Local Development

For local development, run PostgreSQL and Mailpit with Docker Compose, and run the FastAPI and Vite development servers locally.

Start the supporting services:

```bash
docker compose up -d db mailpit
```

Then, from the `backend` directory, install the dependencies and prepare the database:

```bash
uv sync
uv run bash scripts/prestart.sh
```

Start the FastAPI development server:

```bash
uv run fastapi dev
```

In another terminal, from the project root, install the frontend dependencies and start the Vite development server:

```bash
bun install
bun run dev
```

Now you can open these URLs:

Frontend development server: <http://localhost:5173>

Backend API: <http://localhost:8000>

Automatic interactive API documentation with Swagger UI: <http://localhost:8000/docs>

Mailpit: <http://localhost:8025>

The frontend development server uses the backend at `http://localhost:8000`, as configured in `frontend/.env`.

bun run build

# Full Stack FastAPI Template

[![Test Docker Compose](../../actions/workflows/test-docker-compose.yml/badge.svg)](../../actions/workflows/test-docker-compose.yml)
[![Test Backend](../../actions/workflows/test-backend.yml/badge.svg)](../../actions/workflows/test-backend.yml)

## Technology Stack and Features

- ⚡ [**FastAPI**](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com) for the Python backend API.
  - 🧰 [SQLModel](https://sqlmodel.tiangolo.com) for the Python SQL database interactions (ORM).
  - 🔍 [Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev), used by FastAPI, for the data validation and settings management.
  - 💾 [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org) as the SQL database.
- 🚀 [React](https://react.dev) for the frontend.
  - 🧩 Built into the backend application and served by FastAPI on the same domain as the API.
  - 💃 Using TypeScript, hooks, [Vite](https://vitejs.dev), and other parts of a modern frontend stack.
  - 🎨 [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com) and [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com) for the frontend components.
  - 🤖 An automatically generated frontend client.
  - 🧪 [Playwright](https://playwright.dev) for end-to-end testing.
  - 🦇 Dark mode support.
- ☁️ [FastAPI Cloud](https://fastapicloud.com) for deployment.
- 🐋 [Docker Compose](https://www.docker.com) for local services and self-hosted deployment.
  - 📞 [Traefik](https://traefik.io) as a reverse proxy with automatic HTTPS.
- 🔒 Secure password hashing by default.
- 🔑 JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication.
- 📫 Email-based password recovery.
- ✉️ [React Email](https://react.email) for email templates.
- 📬 [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) for local email testing during development.
- ✅ Tests with [Pytest](https://pytest.org).
- 🏭 CI (continuous integration) and CD (continuous deployment) based on GitHub Actions.

### Dashboard Login

![Dashboard login screenshot](img/login.png)

### Dashboard - Admin

![Admin dashboard screenshot](img/dashboard.png)

### Dashboard - Items

![Items dashboard screenshot](img/dashboard-items.png)

### Dashboard - Dark Mode

![Dark mode dashboard screenshot](img/dashboard-dark.png)

### React Email Templates

![Email templates screenshot](img/react-email.png)

### Mailpit - Local Email Testing

![Mailpit screenshot](img/mailpit.png)

### Interactive API Documentation

![API docs](img/docs.png)

## How to Use It

Click the **Use this template** button at the top of this page to create a new repository.

## Backend Development

Backend docs: [backend/README.md](./backend/README.md).

## Frontend Development

Frontend docs: [frontend/README.md](./frontend/README.md).

## Deployment

FastAPI Cloud deployment: [deployment.md](./deployment.md).

Self-hosted deployment with Docker Compose: [deployment-docker-compose.md](./deployment-docker-compose.md).

## Development

General development docs: [development.md](./development.md).

This includes the local FastAPI and Vite workflow, Docker Compose services, `.env` configuration, and more.

## Release Notes

Check the file [release-notes.md](./release-notes.md).

## License

The Full Stack FastAPI Template is licensed under the terms of the MIT license.

- **Not useful:** the `sqlmodel` skill has nothing on Alembic, so the migration from `is_superuser` to roles gets written by hand. Nothing anywhere covers frontend route guards; we'll follow the template's existing `beforeLoad` pattern.

- **In:** a role model with three levels (Admin, Manager, Member), a database migration, backend enforcement, matching frontend behaviour, a stub metrics page, focused security tests, a way to try all three roles locally, and the submission files.
- **Out:** unrelated refactoring, infrastructure, visual polish, extra docs and diagrams, agent configuration, and any merge to `master`.

**Requirements**
- **Admin** manages users and their access.
- **Manager** can view users and metrics but cannot change access.
- **Member** can only view and update their own profile.

- The database is already populated: existing `is_superuser` users must migrate with no privilege change, and the downgrade must be safe.

from collections.abc import Generator
from typing import Annotated

import jwt
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer
from jwt.exceptions import InvalidTokenError
from pydantic import ValidationError
from sqlmodel import Session

from app.core import security
from app.core.config import settings
from app.core.db import engine
from app.models import TokenPayload, User

reusable_oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(
    tokenUrl=f"{settings.API_V1_STR}/login/access-token"
)


def get_db() -> Generator[Session]:
    with Session(engine) as session:
        yield session


SessionDep = Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)]
TokenDep = Annotated[str, Depends(reusable_oauth2)]


def get_current_user(session: SessionDep, token: TokenDep) -> User:
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(
            token, settings.SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[security.ALGORITHM]
        )
        token_data = TokenPayload(**payload)
    except InvalidTokenError, ValidationError:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN,
            detail="Could not validate credentials",
        )
    user = session.get(User, token_data.sub)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="User not found")
    if not user.is_active:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Inactive user")
    return user


CurrentUser = Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)]


def get_current_active_superuser(current_user: CurrentUser) -> User:
    if not current_user.is_superuser:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=403, detail="The user doesn't have enough privileges"
        )
    return current_user

content.text:
# Architecture: role-based access

**Status**
- ✅ Read the current auth code (backend checks and frontend guards)
- ✅ Designed the role and permission model and the migration
- ✅ Mapped the happy paths and edge cases
- ⏳ Waiting on your sign-off on 6 decisions
- ❌ One existing bug blocks the Manager role (finding 3 below)

## What the current code does
1. The token carries only the user id. Every request reloads the user from the database, so a change to someone's role or active status applies on their next request. Role must therefore stay out of the token.
2. The "superuser" check is hard-coded in 4 route files and in about 6 places in the frontend.
3. ❌ The frontend logs the user out on any 403. The backend also answers 403 for a bad token. So a Manager who opens an Admin-only action would get logged out.
4. A deactivated user gets 400, which the frontend ignores. They stay on a half-broken screen instead of being logged out.

## The model, built for live rule changes
- **Role** is one new column on the user: `admin` / `manager` / `member`. It's a plain text column with a database check on allowed values, not a native Postgres enum, so adding a role later is a one-line change.
- **Permissions** are a fixed list in code: `users:read`, `users:manage`, `metrics:read`, `items:read_all`, `system:admin`.
- **One table maps each role to its permissions.** This is the single source of truth. A live rule change means editing one line here plus one test.
- **Each backend endpoint declares the permission it needs**, through one shared check. No route checks a role name directly.
- **The current-user response gains a `permissions` list.** The frontend gates pages, menu items and buttons on that list, never on role names. So a rule change needs no frontend edit.

## Role permission matrix

| Action | Admin | Manager | Member |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| View or update own profile, change own password | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Delete own account | ❌¹ | ✅ | ✅ |
| List users, view any user | ✅ | ✅ (read-only) | ❌ (own only) |
| Create, update or delete users; change role or active status | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Metrics page (stub) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Items: own | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Items: all users' | ✅² | ❌ | ❌ |
| Test email, password-recovery preview | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Public signup | always creates a Member | | |

¹ Kept from today's behaviour, and it protects the last admin.
² Same as what superusers can do today, so nothing changes for them.

## Migration, run against the 2k-user database
**Phase 1 (this PR).** Postgres runs it in one transaction:
1. Add the `role` column, allowing empty values at first.
2. Set `role = admin` where `is_superuser` is true, and `member` for everyone else.
3. Make `role` required, default it to `member` and add the check on allowed values.

The migration then fails itself unless the number of admins equals the number of superusers before it ran. That guarantees no privilege changes, in either direction.

Keeping `is_superuser`:
- The column stays in the database and the app keeps it in sync on every write (`is_superuser = role is admin`). That keeps a code rollback safe.
- The API no longer accepts it as input. Unknown fields are silently ignored, so an old client can't use it to escalate.

**Downgrade** drops `role`. Admins stay superusers, and Managers drop back to regular users. Nobody gains privileges.

**Phase 2** (a later release, out of scope): drop `is_superuser`. I'll note it in the README.

## Sessions and error handling (fixes findings 3 and 4)
- **401** means "not authenticated": bad or expired token, deleted user, or deactivated user. The frontend logs the user out.
- **403** means "authenticated but not allowed". The frontend shows a message and redirects home, without logging out.
- On a 403, the frontend reloads the current user, so its menus pick up a role change made mid-session.
- The login endpoint keeps its current 400 for a wrong password or an inactive user.

## Scenarios
**Happy paths**
- An existing superuser deploys into Admin and keeps every right they had.
- An existing user becomes a Member and loses nothing.
- An Admin promotes a Member to Manager. On their next request, the Manager sees Users (read-only) and Metrics.
- A Manager browses users and metrics, and the edit buttons are hidden.
- A Member signs up, edits their profile, and only sees their own items.

**Edge cases** (🔒 means it gets an automated test)
- 🔒 A Manager calls the user-update endpoint directly to change someone's role → 403.
- 🔒 A Member sends `role` or `is_active` in their own profile update → ignored. That's the mass-assignment case.
- 🔒 Someone sends a role at signup → ignored; they become a Member.
- 🔒 An Admin is demoted or deactivated while logged in → their next request is 403 or 401.
- 🔒 The last active admin can't be demoted, deactivated or deleted → 409. Two admins demoting each other at once are handled by locking the admin rows in the transaction.
- An admin can't change their own role or active status through the admin screen, which prevents self-lockout.
- A user with no permission opens `/admin` or `/metrics` by URL → redirected home with a message, not logged out.
- A user is deleted while their token is still valid → 401 → logged out.
- A Manager reads another user by id → allowed. A Member does the same → 403.
- The migration runs on an empty or partly populated database → the count check still holds.

## Trying all three roles locally
The local seed creates `admin@` (the existing first superuser), plus `manager@example.com` and `member@example.com`. It only runs when the environment is `local`, and their passwords come from the env file.

## Your call, defaults in bold
1. **Admin** keeps seeing all users' items, as superusers do today. The alternative is own items only.
2. **Managers** see users' role and active status, read-only.
3. **The last-admin and self-lockout guards** are in scope. They're small and security-critical.
4. **401 vs 403** gets split as above. A few existing tests that expect 403 for a bad token will change.
5. **`is_superuser`** follows the two-phase plan: kept and synced now, dropped in a later release.
6. **Demo accounts** are seeded only in the `local` environment.

Nothing has started yet. This is my reading of your dictation, so please correct anything I've got wrong.

**1. Goal**
- Deliver the role-based access feature as if the app were in production: 2,000 existing users, no access to production, nothing merged to `master`.
- The main deliverable is evidence that it works before anything is deployed. That means automated tests, but also scenario runs per role and a migration rehearsal.
- The migration rehearsal would run against a populated copy of the database: upgrade, check counts, downgrade, upgrade again, and confirm no one's privileges changed.
- Names, folder structure and file names should be precise and clear. You consider that part of the review.
- The matrix is approved. We keep `is_superuser` for now, and keep the guard that stops the last admin from being removed. Any admin can still remove any other admin as long as one stays.

**2. Delivery: two PRs from me**
- **PR 1:** add the `role` column, the permission checks, the frontend changes, the tests, and the README updates (assumptions, how to run, the three demo roles).
- **PR 2:** drop `is_superuser`. It merges either in a later deploy or together with PR 1 if a short outage is acceptable. The README would describe both options.

**3. Workflow: two local conductors**
- **Me (build):** I write the code and open both PRs.
- **Second session (verify):** a separate local session that writes and runs the scenario checks and the migration rehearsal. It would keep its files in its own clearly named folder, for example `backend/tests/scenarios/` plus a migration rehearsal script, and report pass or fail per scenario.
- **Why two:** verification runs in parallel, so our conversation isn't blocked while tests run.
- **Order:** first we agree a development plan that says which files each conductor owns and how results flow back. Only then does either of us start.
- **AI exports:** the raw transcripts from both sessions go into `ai-conversations/`.

**4. Requirements you may be missing**
- ❌ **Time limit.** The task asks for about one hour and for the time actually spent. This scope, with two conductors, two PRs and a migration rehearsal, will clearly run over. The task also says "no bonus for … a large number of tests". We should either accept going over and say so honestly in the README, or trim.
- ⏳ **Scope control is graded.** The verification folder must stay lean, or it reads as over-engineering.
- ⏳ **"Provide only".** Two PRs are fine if the README links them and explains the order.
- **Security points I'd add to the plan:**
  - Tokens stay valid for 8 days, which is acceptable because the user is reloaded from the database on every request.
  - Password recovery must not work for deactivated users.
  - A Member asking for another user's record should get 403, which doesn't reveal whether that user exists.

4. Should the second conductor write only verification files and never touch app code? That's my default.

---
name: Migrations Convention
status: stable
purpose: How DB migrations are written, applied, and gated — the conductor may apply them, but only on explicit human confirmation for that specific apply.
---

# Migrations

For any repo holding versioned SQL under a migrations directory. Covers who applies a
migration, how the files are written, and what belongs in the schema at all.

## The apply gate

**The conductor applies migrations — always — on the human's confirmation for that specific
apply. The human never applies one by hand.** The rule in the founder's words (2026-08-25):
*"HUMAN confirm — conductor applies. If no credentials — check and report to human."*
Conductor-apply is not one option among several; it replaced human-migrate outright. The
transport is whatever the session holds — a database MCP server, a repo apply script, the vendor
CLI, or a dispatchable CI workflow — and a session holding none has a credential to be
provisioned, not a human to hand the SQL to.

- **State what is pending, plainly**: WHICH files, WHAT they change in one line, WHICH database
  (project or environment name). A prod/dev mix-up must be visible in that sentence, not
  discoverable afterwards.
- **Take the affirmative in the normal flow of work, however it is phrased** — "apply", "go",
  "merge and apply" are all a yes. Never block the human with a formatted interrogation, never
  demand the answer in your shape, never re-ask for ceremony's sake.
- **Confirmation is affirmative, never assumed** — the session-discipline rule in `CLAUDE.md`
  applies here with no softening. Silence, a topic change, and the go given for the previous
  apply are all not-a-yes. One apply, one confirmation.
- **No affirmative yet is not a blocker.** Carry on with everything else and leave the pending
  apply visible in your report; it waits, you don't.
- **CI-driven apply stays valid.** Where a pipeline applies on merge, the human's merge
  approval IS the confirmation — don't ask twice, and never hand-apply around the pipeline.
- **No credentials → report the provisioning ask.** Test the transports, then tell the human
  exactly what to provision — a repo secret the dispatchable workflow reads, or a session env
  credential — and carry on with other work meanwhile. **Never ask the human to apply it
  himself.** Hand application (pasting SQL into a console, running `psql` by hand) is banned as
  a workflow: it is what conductor-apply replaced, not a fallback beneath it. A repo with no
  transport has a provisioning gap to close, not a manual door to open.

**Test an externally-grounded claim before you act on it.** Delete-first keeps in-repo claims
true by construction. Claims about external state drift with no commit to trigger it — so test
those before acting, and correct them in the same change. External here means a database's
reachability, a remote branch's existence, a platform flag, an installed tool: try it (list
tables, dry-run, `git ls-remote`) rather than trusting the sentence. Verification is never a
license to route around a wrong doc and leave it standing — the correction is one dated positive
statement of what is true now. Precedent: a repo README asserted no egress and no CLI while that
same session provably held two working transports.

Any repo-local "humans apply the migrations" text is superseded by this convention — delete it,
whether it rests on a stale transport claim or on habit. The only automation-side variant that
stands is a pipeline that applies on merge (above), recorded as a divergence in the repo's own
copy. A developer running the CLI against a local or dev database while building is ordinary
development, not the banned path: what is banned is hand application as the way a change reaches
a real database.

## Migration files

- **Forward-only.** A change of course is a new file, never an edit of an applied one.
- **Idempotent.** Re-running every file in filename order converges on the same state:
  `if not exists`, `drop … if exists` + recreate, `on conflict do nothing`.
- **`<timestamp>_<description>.sql`**, in the repo's migrations directory (`supabase/migrations/`
  where the vendor sets it). First segment digits only, so filename order is apply order.
- **Every file opens with a header comment**: what it changes, why, and the ruling or task it
  serves. The file is the only place a future reader gets the reason.
- **One concern per file.** Separate schema (DDL) from data moves (DML); isolate destructive
  drops into their own later file.
- **Dry-run first** where the tool offers one, then apply.
- **Verify by read-back, not by exit code.** A guarded statement that no-ops still exits 0, so
  a clean green apply is not evidence the change landed — query the object back. Run the
  platform's security/performance advisors after apply where they exist.

## Editing an applied migration

Forbidden by default. One blessed exception:

**When an idempotency guard in an old file would silently RESURRECT state that a newer file
drops, on a full in-order re-run.** The guard makes an in-place edit of an already-applied
object a no-op, so the old block keeps re-adding what the newer file then removes — a fresh
apply and a re-apply end up in different states. Fix: delete the offending block from the old
file and let the newer file's drop stand alone. (Precedent: a superseded event-name constraint,
2026-08-25.)

Using the exception requires recording it twice, or it is just an edit:

1. **Where the block was** — a comment in the old file saying what was removed and why.
2. **In the migrations README** — dated, with the "a later file's DROP would otherwise race a
   resurrected object" justification spelled out.

No other edit rides this precedent without the same justification.

## Schema vs data

The database enforces **structure** and **closed grouping axes** — the axes reports group by,
such as a channel enum. It does not enumerate **product-iterating data lists**, such as event
names. Those live in code: a typed union plus a runtime allow-list at the API edge, with at
most a format-sanity constraint database-side. (Founder ruling, 2026-08-25.)

**Test: does adding a value require a product decision or a schema decision?** Product decision
→ code. Schema decision → database.

Why it matters: a value list inside a CHECK constraint turns every product iteration into a
migration plus an apply gate, and the constraint fails closed — the new value is rejected in
production before anyone notices the list needs a release.

## Schema truth

- Where the repo consumes DB types in code, **generate them from the live schema** and commit
  the output. Generated types are the schema's face in code; hand-written mirrors drift.
- Otherwise the **migrations directory plus its README** is the record. That README lists the
  files in order, what each creates, and the invariants a new file must not break.

## Related

- `docs/conventions/good-docs.md` — the migrations README is a doc; write it to that standard.
- `docs/conventions/good-conduct.md` — the conductor's dispatch and escalation rules; a
  destructive or scope-changing action goes to the human, no agent gate.

---

# Conductor Doctrine

Are you the conductor? If you report to the human, yes — this doc is for you. If you report to another agent, you are a sub-agent, and this doc is not for you.

Doctrine for any conductor, in any harness (Claude Code, Cursor). Load it from every conductor surface: the `/conduct` and `/deep-thinking` commands, and the skill parent-conductors (`article`, `maintainance`, `deep-engineering`, `localization`). The commands slim to operational runbooks; the doctrine — responsibilities, patterns, dispatch rules — lives here, once.

## Conductor responsibilities

You manage the workflow; you do not do the work in your own thread.

1. **Think on the workflow** — the workflow design is YOUR work; the tasks inside it are not. Decompose, sequence, decide who runs.
2. **Keep your own context clean** — delegate any routine a sub-agent can carry; don't burn your window on work an executor should hold.
3. **Know your tooling arms** — the agent roster (`.claude/agents/README.md`) and the skills. You can't staff a workflow with agents you don't know exist.
4. **Track dispatched agents** — who is running, what each owes you back, what's still open.
5. **Own the communication with Vasyl** — its quality is yours, not an agent's. See `good-communication.md`.

## The 10 agentic patterns

Provenance meaning: `[industry]` = a canonical published pattern — training data carries the detail; `[ours]` = exists nowhere else — this table is the only source.

| # | Pattern | Shape | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One agent first | Don't spawn a team when one well-briefed agent suffices; multi-agent buys only context isolation, parallelism, or specialization. | industry — OpenAI agents guide; Anthropic |
| 2 | Architect before execution | Above the floor, a general-purpose architect agent drafts the design before any executor writes. Review the design TWICE: an `onoma` pass (precise names, correct categories) and a layering pass (would fresh categories give better boundaries?). | ours |
| 3 | Decompose by lane | Chunk by delivery lane one agent can own end-to-end: FE, BE, db-migration, copy + localization, UX/UI mocking + visual verification (mock and real app). | ours |
| 4 | Brief like a manager | Every dispatch states goal + why, what's ruled out, exact paths, output format; never delegate the understanding you owe (`good-prompting.md`). | industry — Anthropic multi-agent research system |
| 5 | Executor+reviewer couple per chunk | Above the floor: 2 agents, 3 steps — executor produces → fresh independent reviewer returns verdict (`pass \| revise \| escalate`) + numbered findings → executor applies. | ours |
| 6 | Staff to task size | 1 agent for a lookup; 2–4 for a comparison; 3–5 parallel for a sweep; never over-staff. | industry — Anthropic |
| 7 | Reviewers judge, never fix | The reviewer's job is to find what's wrong (build/lint fails, missed requirement, wrong claim), not to agree — verdict + findings only; a reviewer who edits stops being independent. | industry — generator–critic |
| 8 | Separate review ends every substantial workflow | A final pass by an agent that did none of the work, before the conductor accepts. | ours |
| 9 | Fat Tony before Vasyl | An unclear situation or design question goes to `essence-finder` (aka Fat Tony) first; only surviving questions escalate to the human. Boundary: destructive actions, scope changes, and permissions go straight to the human — no agent gate. | ours |
| 10 | Conductor owns the disk | Sub-agents propose (own scratch files / envelopes); the conductor applies, verifies with the domain gate, commits. That commit also deletes whatever it made outdated — content plus references — never a later cleanup task. | industry framing + repo convention |

## The complexity floor

Patterns 2 and 5 govern work that requires diligence — multiple files, a requirement to meet, or a claim to check. A small mechanical change takes a single executor, no architect. A trivial edit (one-line rename, typo) the conductor does directly and NAMES the exception, so the exception isn't abused.

## Shared dispatch rules

- State the decomposition in 3–5 lines before dispatching.
- Parallelize independent dispatches in ONE message with multiple Agent calls — disjoint outputs only (each writes its own file); never fan parallel writers onto one shared file.
- Sequence dependent jobs — job B waits on job A's accepted output, then B is briefed with it.
- Loop to convergence, not a count — cap ≈3 cycles as a BACKSTOP, then escalate; never force a pass. `revise` → re-brief the executor with the numbered findings, re-review. `escalate` → surface to the human; don't paper over it.
- You own the synthesis — never "based on the agents' output, decide."
- Report in MINTO (`good-communication.md`).

## Related

- `docs/conventions/good-prompting.md` — how to brief an agent (patterns 1, 4).
- `docs/conventions/good-communication.md` — MINTO reporting (responsibility 5).
- `.claude/agents/README.md` — the agent roster and its mechanics (responsibility 3).

model: sonnet

You name one entity per invocation — a code entity or an agent — so a future reader can predict what it holds or does **without opening its definition**. The conductor's description of the entity is a **hypothesis**. Verify it against the code before you name anything.

- The entity: current name (or "new") + `file:line` (or target file).
- Rename: why — what the current name gets wrong (lies, overclaims, collides, stale).
- New entity: the wider purpose — human intent, the epic/task it belongs to, what calls it (or will), its module.
- Hard constraints: words that must / must-not appear.

Missing and not cheaply recoverable from code → **stop and ask**, don't guess.

## Method — every step, cite `file:line`

1. **Read the definition.** What it holds, what it's derived from, what it does.
2. **Read every consumer.** Grep the symbol; for each call site, what is it used for? A name must fit the contract, not just the definition.
3. **Read the system context.**
   - Module purpose + boundary: README / `index.ts` barrel / file header.
   - **Encapsulated** (module-private) or **public** (exported across a barrier) — this changes the audience, therefore the name.
   - The naming neighborhood: siblings in the same file and barrel. Match casing, plurality, prefix/suffix grammar.
4. **Articulate the KIND before reaching for a word.** The kind dictates the vocabulary slot. Distinctions to make consciously (not exhaustive — articulate the relevant ones):
   - **title** vs **label** vs **name** vs **id** — title is canonical user-facing; label is what a control/element is called; name is identification; id is technical uniqueness.
   - **registry** vs **catalog** vs **map** vs **table** vs **list** — registry is authoritative source of truth; catalog enumerates; map keys→values; table is relational; list is ordered. The kind dictates the suffix.
   - **route** vs **path** vs **url** vs **slug** vs **link** — layers of one concept; mixing them produces lies.
   - **event** vs **handler** vs **callback**; **config** vs **settings** vs **preferences**; **resolver** vs **getter** vs **factory**; etc.

   Can't state the KIND → can't name it. Ask the conductor.

Optimize for orthogonality + memorability, not predict-from-name; Greek/Latin/Ukrainian roots and coined words (`namesmith`) are all equally good.
Judge collision in the handle's own namespace — human↔conductor chat in this repo; an outside product sharing the name matters only if it's part of this repo's world.
Everyday-word collision is judged against this human's working vocabulary, not native-English frequency; famous proper names (`rodin`, `cicero`) don't collide — fame is not a defect.

# DB Guide: Full‑stack feature workflow (Supabase + Next.js)

## Purpose

Agreed workflow to design, migrate, and wire DB‑backed features safely and repeatably. This is
Brizzy's single local home for database truth — schema, access, and migration mechanics
(consolidated 2026-08-25).

## Layering — one truth, one home

`docs/conventions/good-migrations.md` is the canon, synced from the harness hub. It owns the
rules that hold in every repo: forward-only idempotent files, timestamp naming, the apply gate,
editing an applied migration, schema-vs-data, where schema truth lives. **Read it first.**

This file owns Brizzy's instantiation only — the two databases, the CLIs, the CI pipeline, the
risky-change playbook. A repo file never restates the canon it cites; if a rule here also holds
elsewhere, it belongs upstream, not in both.

## Principles

- Keep app schema thin and future‑proof: prefer a few stable columns over many fields.
- App reads identity from `auth.users`; app profile is `public.profiles` with public read, self‑edit only.
- Treat Storage like a CDN with RLS; store object keys (not URLs) in tables.
- Prefer triggers for lifecycle defaults (e.g., seed profiles on signup, update timestamps).

## Repositories & Files

- Migrations live in `supabase/migrations/`; the Supabase CLI is the canonical interface.
  - Example: `20251002133000_user_setup_updated_at_trigger.sql`
- Generated types: `src/types/supabase-db.ts`, via `npm run gen-db-types`.
- App code uses `@/utils/supabase/client` and `@/utils/supabase/server` (SSR cookies).
- API helpers live in `src/app/api/_shared/api.utils.ts`; see `src/app/api/good-api.md` for usage conventions.

## Standard Feature Flow

1. Plan (1-2 bullets)

- Data model changes (tables/columns/constraints)
- Access model (RLS policies)
- Storage needs (buckets/policies) if any

2. Write the SQL migration — file rules per the convention; include what the feature needs:
   columns, indexes, triggers, policies, buckets.

3. Apply to DEV — see § Migrations, Brizzy specifics below.

4. Wire UI/API

- Read with server/client Supabase helpers
- Write via minimal upserts/updates; rely on triggers for timestamps
- Validate inputs client‑side; rely on RLS on server

5. Verify

- Quick sanity queries (copy/paste in SQL Editor):
  - `select * from public.profiles limit 5;`
  - `select count(*) from storage.objects where bucket_id = 'avatars';`
- Test from the app: login, CRUD, storage download

6. Security check

- RLS ON for all tables holding user data (gate by `auth.uid()`).
- Public reads: base-table `SELECT` policies (Option A; no views).
- Storage policies match visibility needs.

## Migrations — Brizzy specifics

**Two databases**: **Brizzy_DEV** (local work and PR checks) and **Brizzy_PROD** (updated only
by CI on merge to `main`).

**Naming**: CI enforces the canon's naming with `^[0-9]+_.+\.sql$`.

**Tooling**: CLI login uses a repo secret token in CI; locally you are linked to Brizzy_DEV.
The project runs **two CLIs** — the npm package (drives `gen-db-types`) and a global install
(direct commands). Keep both current.

### Local development (Brizzy_DEV)

1. **Plan.** Minimal DDL; if data moves, plan a separate DML file.
2. **Create.** `supabase migration new <short-name>`, `supabase db diff -f <short-name>`, or
   hand-write the file.
3. **Apply.** `supabase db push`, then `supabase db push --dry-run` → “up to date”, then
   `supabase migration list` → newest file shows `applied`. Who may run this is the
   convention's apply gate: a conductor holding the CLI applies only on Vasyl's explicit
   confirmation for that specific apply. Driving the CLI against Brizzy_DEV while building is
   ordinary development — the canon's ban is on hand application as the way a change reaches
   PROD, which here only ever happens through the pipeline below.
4. **Commit** the migration **with the app code** that depends on it, same PR.

### CI & promotion

On PR (into `develop` or `main`):

- Filename check against the pattern above.
- DEV verification: dry-run plan against Brizzy_DEV, then apply; print `migration list`.
- Types sync: regenerate `src/types/supabase-db.ts` from linked DEV. Same-repo PRs get an
  auto-commit; forks get a printed diff and a failure — fix locally with `npm run gen-db-types`.
- Destructive plan (any `DROP`) requires the PR label **`db/drop-approved`**.

On merge to `main`: PROD dry-run → apply to Brizzy_PROD. **The merge approval IS the apply
confirmation** for this path (per the convention's CI clause) — nobody asks again, and nobody
hand-applies to PROD around the pipeline. Destructive changes are blocked by default and need
the workflow's explicit approval path. Concurrency: CI cancels overlapping runs per branch, so
a double-apply cannot race.

### Risky changes

- **Two-phase rename / shape change**: add the new shape and backfill → ship code reading it →
  drop the old shape in a later migration once stable.
- **Backfills**: wrap in `BEGIN; … COMMIT;` where atomicity helps; guard every step.
- **Destructive ops**: carry the `db/drop-approved` label; PROD needs the workflow's approval
  path on top.

### RLS, seeds, recovery, audit

- Every policy, grant and role lives in a migration; validate on DEV via PR CI, and run a
  DEV-vs-PROD parity review after a PROD deploy.
- DEV-only seed data belongs in scripts/fixtures — never in a PROD migration, never test users.
- Recovery: Supabase PRO automated backups are the emergency path; otherwise forward-fix.
- Ledger: Supabase Dashboard → Database → Migrations → History. CI logs (plan, apply,
  `migration list`) are the deployment audit.

### Command cheat sheet

- New migration: `supabase migration new <thing>` · from diff: `supabase db diff -f <name>`
- Apply to the current link: `supabase db push` · dry-run: `supabase db push --dry-run`
- History: `supabase migration list`
- Types: `npm run gen-db-types`
- CLI upkeep: `npm update supabase` (npm) · `brew upgrade supabase` (global, macOS)

## Local Dev Tips

- Use `storage.download(path)` for images to avoid Next image domain config
- If switching to public URLs later, use `getPublicUrl(path)` and add domain to Next `images.remotePatterns`

## Checklist for PRs touching DB

- [ ] Migration SQL added under `supabase/migrations/`
- [ ] Doc updated here with intended behavior
- [ ] RLS enabled; policies minimal and correct
- [ ] UI validates inputs; writes are minimal
- [ ] Tested sign‑in, read, write, storage download

## Related

- `docs/conventions/good-migrations.md` — the canon this file instantiates.
- `.cursor/rules/28-db.mdc` — loads both on schema/Supabase context, plus the MCP workflow.

4. Wire UI/API

- Read with server/client Supabase helpers
- Write via minimal upserts/updates; rely on triggers for timestamps
- Validate inputs client‑side; rely on RLS on server

5. Verify

- Quick sanity queries (copy/paste in SQL Editor):
  - `select * from public.profiles limit 5;`
  - `select count(*) from storage.objects where bucket_id = 'avatars';`
- Test from the app: login, CRUD, storage download

6. Security check

- RLS ON for all tables holding user data (gate by `auth.uid()`).
- Public reads: base-table `SELECT` policies (Option A; no views).
- Storage policies match visibility needs.

## Migrations — Brizzy specifics

**Two databases**: **Brizzy_DEV** (local work and PR checks) and **Brizzy_PROD** (updated only
by CI on merge to `main`).

**Naming**: CI enforces the canon's naming with `^[0-9]+_.+\.sql$`.

**Tooling**: CLI login uses a repo secret token in CI; locally you are linked to Brizzy_DEV.
The project runs **two CLIs** — the npm package (drives `gen-db-types`) and a global install
(direct commands). Keep both current.

### Local development (Brizzy_DEV)

1. **Plan.** Minimal DDL; if data moves, plan a separate DML file.
2. **Create.** `supabase migration new <short-name>`, `supabase db diff -f <short-name>`, or
   hand-write the file.
3. **Apply.** `supabase db push`, then `supabase db push --dry-run` → “up to date”, then
   `supabase migration list` → newest file shows `applied`. Who may run this is the
   convention's apply gate: a conductor holding the CLI applies only on Vasyl's explicit
   confirmation for that specific apply. Driving the CLI against Brizzy_DEV while building is
   ordinary development — the canon's ban is on hand application as the way a change reaches
   PROD, which here only ever happens through the pipeline below.
4. **Commit** the migration **with the app code** that depends on it, same PR.

### CI & promotion

On PR (into `develop` or `main`):

- Filename check against the pattern above.
- DEV verification: dry-run plan against Brizzy_DEV, then apply; print `migration list`.
- Types sync: regenerate `src/types/supabase-db.ts` from linked DEV. Same-repo PRs get an
  auto-commit; forks get a printed diff and a failure — fix locally with `npm run gen-db-types`.
- Destructive plan (any `DROP`) requires the PR label **`db/drop-approved`**.

On merge to `main`: PROD dry-run → apply to Brizzy_PROD. **The merge approval IS the apply
confirmation** for this path (per the convention's CI clause) — nobody asks again, and nobody
hand-applies to PROD around the pipeline. Destructive changes are blocked by default and need
the workflow's explicit approval path. Concurrency: CI cancels overlapping runs per branch, so
a double-apply cannot race.

### Risky changes

- **Two-phase rename / shape change**: add the new shape and backfill → ship code reading it →
  drop the old shape in a later migration once stable.
- **Backfills**: wrap in `BEGIN; … COMMIT;` where atomicity helps; guard every step.
- **Destructive ops**: carry the `db/drop-approved` label; PROD needs the workflow's approval
  path on top.

### RLS, seeds, recovery, audit

- Every policy, grant and role lives in a migration; validate on DEV via PR CI, and run a
  DEV-vs-PROD parity review after a PROD deploy.
- DEV-only seed data belongs in scripts/fixtures — never in a PROD migration, never test users.
- Recovery: Supabase PRO automated backups are the emergency path; otherwise forward-fix.
- Ledger: Supabase Dashboard → Database → Migrations → History. CI logs (plan, apply,
  `migration list`) are the deployment audit.

### Command cheat sheet

- New migration: `supabase migration new <thing>` · from diff: `supabase db diff -f <name>`
- Apply to the current link: `supabase db push` · dry-run: `supabase db push --dry-run`
- History: `supabase migration list`
- Types: `npm run gen-db-types`
- CLI upkeep: `npm update supabase` (npm) · `brew upgrade supabase` (global, macOS)

## Local Dev Tips

- Use `storage.download(path)` for images to avoid Next image domain config
- If switching to public URLs later, use `getPublicUrl(path)` and add domain to Next `images.remotePatterns`

## Checklist for PRs touching DB

- [ ] Migration SQL added under `supabase/migrations/`
- [ ] Doc updated here with intended behavior
- [ ] RLS enabled; policies minimal and correct
- [ ] UI validates inputs; writes are minimal
- [ ] Tested sign‑in, read, write, storage download

## Related

- `docs/conventions/good-migrations.md` — the canon this file instantiates.
- `.cursor/rules/28-db.mdc` — loads both on schema/Supabase context, plus the MCP workflow.

- **Final review.** One last pass by an agent that did none of the work.
- **Evidence goes in the PR descriptions**, not the README: scenario results and migration rehearsal output, ready to talk through in the interview.

## Two conductors

| Phase | Me (build, main) | Verification session |
|---|---|---|
| **0 · Align** | Lock the decisions and run the `onoma` naming pass. Write the verification brief: the scenario list, which files it owns, and the report format. | Not started. |
| **1 · Data** | Backend model, the permission table, and the three migration files. | **Migration rehearsal:** load a test database with about 2,000 users (admins, regular users, some deactivated). Then upgrade, compare counts, downgrade and upgrade again. |
| **2 · API** | Switch endpoints to permission checks. Return 401 for bad, deleted or deactivated sessions and 403 for denied access. Add the last-admin guard and the local demo seed. | Write tests that follow the scenario list, one ID per scenario. Run them against my branch and report pass or fail per ID. |
| **3 · UI** | Role picker, menus and buttons driven by permissions, page guards, metrics stub, regenerated API client. | Browser flows per role: opening a forbidden page by URL, Manager seeing read-only screens, a user deactivated mid-session getting logged out. |

| **5 · PR 2** | Branch from PR 1: drop `is_superuser` in code and database. | Rehearse PR 2's migration (up and down), rerun everything, then do the final independent review. |
| **6 · Wrap** | README: assumptions, commands, time spent. Export the raw transcripts. | Export its own raw transcript. |

**How the two of us work together**
- We share this checkout but never touch the same files.
- The verification session writes only its own tests and the rehearsal script, and commits nothing. I review and commit its files into the right PR, as the harness's conductor rules require.
